The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return zero-based indexes i,j of any two distinct positions whose values sum to target. Return -1,-1 if no pair exists; either order of a valid pair is accepted. The visible fixture is `[6, 4, 9, 7] target=13` and its example result is `1,2`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

For the visible input `[6, 4, 9, 7] target=13`, the stated result is `1,2`. Before reading code, name the smallest piece of information that must survive from one step to the next. That is the mental model for Complement Lookup; it gives you a reason for each update instead of a line of code to memorise.

The core mechanism is this: For each number, ask whether target - number has already appeared. Treat it as a claim to test after every operation. Write down the state before the first operation, update it once, and ask which part of the claim is still true.
